About 100 years before this catchy song, Hannah Whitall Smith wrote an ageless book called, The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life. In it, she detailed a powerful formula for happy living that was based on complete faith in God and fully surrendering to His will. The message in the song and the book are the same, except the book gives us solid “how to” perspectives for Christians. While we won’t be singing the song or reviewing the book, we will be applying scriptural principles that will help make happiness real in our daily Christian lives.

This is a bold subject considering how much of the world is either at war or on the edge of war. The planet is sick, the people are miserable and dying, the news is grim, graphic and grotesque. How can we speak of happiness at a time like this? Does God even want us to be happy?

We’ll first have to define what happiness means. Generally, we think of it as temporary positive emotion, as in: we wish someone “Happy Birthday,” and there is excitement as they blow candles out on a cake, and then it’s over as we move on to the next problem of life. But we want to see how the Bible defines being happy. What is Christian happiness? It may not be what you expect.

Let’s start with an Old Testament perspective on happiness. We find that “to be happy” and “to be blessed” can be synonymous: Happy: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #835 'esher; (noun) happiness; only in masculine plural construction as {interjection} how happy! - {blessed} happy

The King James Version translates this as: blessed 27 times, happy 15 times

Brown-Driver-Briggs’ Definition: 1) happiness, blessedness

a) often used as interjection, b) blessed are This isn’t a “jumping for joy” kind of emotion. As Val, one of our CQ volunteers says, “This isn’t always laughing like a hyena.” Instead, it has the sense of having a stable well-being. This is the theme we further explore the biblical meaning of happiness.

Deuteronomy 33:29: (KJV) Happy <835> art thou, O Israel: who is like unto thee, O people saved by the LORD, the shield of thy help, and who is the sword of thy excellency! and thine enemies shall be found liars unto thee; and thou shalt tread upon their high places.

Happy art thou, O Israel…O people saved by the Lord - this is a reflection on national happiness in this first verse.

Psalms 1:1-2: 1 How blessed <835> is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand in the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers! 2 But his delight is in the law of the LORD, and in His law he meditates day and night.

Notice how the blessed or happy person isn’t walking, standing or sitting where they don’t belong. (Source: Bible commentary by David Guzik) The righteous man only has God’s word on his mind two times a day: day and night. That about covers it all!

We can see the process: the man who is NOT blessed starts out walking, then he slows down to standing, then he gets comfortable and sits. Christian happiness needs to be focused on always moving forward in God’s word. This happiness or blessedness (in one place the word was translated blessed, one used happy) is a thing – not a feeling. It is a tangible state of mind.

To better understand what this happiness/blessedness is based on, we want to look at the root word, as it gives us a potentially unexpected expansion of meaning. Happy/Blessed: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #833 'ashar; (verb) a primitive root; to be straight (used in the widest sense, especially to be level, right, happy); figuratively, to go forward, be honest, prosper The King James Version translates this word as: blessed 7 times, lead 2 times, go 2 times, guide 1 time, happy 2 times, leaders 1 time, relieve 1 time Brown-Drive-Briggs’ Definition includes: to go straight, walk, go on, advance, make progress To be straight, walk, be level – aren’t we talking about being happy? Yes, we are! The next three scriptures use this word in very different ways:

Psalms 41:1-2: 1 How blessed <835> is he who considers the helpless; the LORD will deliver him in a day of trouble. 2 The LORD will protect him and keep him alive, and he shall be called blessed <833> upon the earth; and do not give him over to the desire of his enemies.

Proverbs 9:6: Forsake your folly and live, and proceed <833> in the way of understanding.

Nothing here talks about happiness. Instead, the same word <833> is translated as proceed. We are supposed to be happy by proceeding? Yes! It gives us a sense of progress and purpose when we move forward.

Isaiah 1:17: (KJV) Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve <833> the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.

Here this same Hebrew word is used to indicate moving forward, having purpose, being constructive – an idea of being level or straight, honest and proper in our ways of dealing with others. These meanings are rather unemotional - not like an exuberant feeling. In summary, the primary Old Testament word for happy <835> comes from a word that has to do with being level, moving forward and progressing <833>. This is probably different than what we normally think of what “happy” means.

From an Old Testament perspective, to be truly “happy” and “blessed” is to have a state of mind that is level and right in which progress is attainable.

Now let’s translate this into New Testament happiness: Happy/Blessed: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3107 makarios; (adjective) a prolonged form of the poetical makar (meaning the same); supremely blest; by extension, fortunate, well off The King James Version translates this word as blessed 44 times, happy 5 times, happier 1 time This adjective is used widely. Here are two examples:

1 Peter 4:14: (KJV) If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy <3107> are ye; for the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you: on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified.

This is interesting because it says, happy are ye, but the person is being reproached for the name of Christ! If this was simply emotional happiness, it would not make sense. Happy (supremely blessed) are ye. We can have an experience that emotionally does not feel good but produces this kind of scriptural happiness.

Titus 2:11-13: 11 For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men, 12 instructing us to deny ungodliness and worldly desires and to live sensibly, righteously and godly in the present age, 13 looking for the blessed <3107> hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Christ Jesus, Blessed: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3106 makarizo; (verb) to beatify, i.e., pronounce (or esteem) fortunate: call blessed, count happy The King James Version translates this word as: call blessed 1 time, count happy 1 time Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: to pronounce blessed

This Greek verb is only used twice in the New Testament:

Luke 1:46-48: 46 And Mary said: My soul exalts the Lord, 47 and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior. 48 For He has had regard for the humble state of His bondslave; for behold, from this time on all generations will count <3106> me blessed <3106>.

This is a proclamation of supreme blessing. Mary, the mother of Jesus, realizes the incredible privilege she has. It becomes a label for her in that all will count me blessed.

James 5:11: (KJV) Behold, we count them happy <3106> which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy.

Those who endure, who cope with trials and traumas and difficulty, are considered supremely blessed. It doesn’t mean they feel great and are superficially happy. Rather, it means God is with them, guiding them forward. This is not a “birthday party” kind of happiness.

Christian happiness is not a state of euphoria, and it is not mere tolerance or acceptance either. Biblical happiness is built squarely upon the foundation of God’s word, God’s will and God’s way being our straight path through life. We are fortunate and well-off when the stability of God’s will is our driving force.

God’s will drives this state of mind through whatever the experiences of life may be. In some ways, the way the Bible describes happiness is surprising. On the other hand, having our happiness in God is NO surprise at all!

A happy Christian life is entirely dependent upon perceiving, understanding and embracing God’s ways. How do we do that?

Now that we know the source of all Christian happiness, we can see this “how to” question is the core of everything. The better we learn the “how to,” the happier our Christian walk will become. Our first point is broad in scope as we will see that a happy Christian life is dependent on our embracing all aspects of our lives as purposed by God. Being unhappy doesn’t mean you are failing as a Christian.

Christians get sad, angry, frustrated – and sometimes we have anxiety or depression that needs professional help. There’s no shame in that. Today we’re talking in broad terms about a way of looking at biblical truths to change the perspective of our thinking; truths that give the Christian stability and assurance, and in turn, happiness.

Just because we may struggle with anxiety or depression doesn’t mean we can’t be a happy Christian.

We can learn to find pieces of this happiness to help us cope with what may be a natural inclination, and to work our way step-by-step to overcoming it. This is not an “all-or- nothing” proposition. We can build Christian happiness in small stages. We are going to follow the context of our theme text in Romans 8. The Apostle Paul built a process for us to find and understand true Christian happiness:

Romans 8:12-13: 12 So then, brethren, we are under obligation, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh 13 for if you are living according to the flesh, you must die; but if by the spirit you are putting to death the deeds of the body, you will live.

How important is it to live by the spirit and not by the flesh? It's the secret to godly happiness. We have purpose and peace and a stable life. Life is good.

Are we following the stable, level road of God’s spirit? Or are we following the back and forth, up and down emotional roller coaster of our flesh? That is why living by the spirit is completely different and is where true Christian happiness can begin. Our first little sentence to help us with the individual pieces of Christian happiness is:

This is pretty simple. Know what you are about. Know the “why” of your life. As we introduce each of these little Christian happiness sentences, we will go back to the Old Testament because this is a “whole Bible” teaching. The Old and New Testaments combined show us how biblical happiness is not euphoric; rather, it has the thought of a stable state of mind.

Psalm 112:1: Praise the LORD! How blessed <835> is the man who fears (reverences) the LORD, who greatly delights in His commandments.

Remember how in Psalms 1:1-2, we had the walk – stand – sit admonition? Here, the one who delights in God’s laws is blessed/happy. We’re going to start seeing a pattern: Happiness comes from knowing and doing what God expects of us. That’s our purpose. It makes sense: in His love for us, He has laid out the best path we should take. When we walk on this even, level ground, we should be able to confidently move forward.

Jesus gave a teaching specifically dedicated to the happiness of our purpose – the Beatitudes:

Matthew 5:1-9: 1 When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up on the mountain; and after he sat down, his disciples came to him. 2 He opened his mouth and began to teach them, saying, 3 Blessed <3107> are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. 4 Blessed <3107> are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. 5 Blessed <3107> are the gentle, for they shall inherit the earth. 6 Blessed <3107> are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. 7 Blessed <3107> are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy. 8 Blessed <3107> are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. 9 Blessed <3107> are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.

What does this have to do with being happy? Let’s look at two examples. Blessed are those who mourn for they shall be comforted. Blessed is the same word translated as happy, describing that level, stable, straight approach to life. Those in mourning, if true followers of God and of Christ, know the big picture. Even though they are in a painful state, they see from a larger perspective and are blessed accordingly. They can have that stable, level approach that says, This hurts, but it’s not permanent.

Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. No man is fully righteous, but Jesus says these are blessed because they are trying to achieve righteousness. They have that sense of having a level, even state of mind that says, There is a direction I need to walk to find this righteousness. It is a beautiful picture of how all this works together.

Our purpose is to live as true followers of Jesus with humility, gentleness and desiring righteousness, all in a merciful and pure way. It is to bring the peace of God wherever we go.

Seeking any and all of these things provides strong points of reference for our character.

If I am not happy, which of these Christian principles am I not following?

When our mind feels unsettled and worried, we can use these points as a kind of filter to see if we are weak in a particular area.

Romans 8:14-15: 14 For all who are being led by the spirit of God, these are sons of God. 15 For you have not received a spirit of slavery leading to fear again, but you have received a spirit of adoption as sons by which we cry out, Abba! Father!

How important is this individual connection? It’s amazing that we are sons of God just like Jesus. It’s important to know our heavenly Father is giving us our life experiences because of this special relationship.

We’re so used to thinking of God as our Father that the importance of this point is often missed. Adam was considered a son before he sinned. Thousands of years would go by before the relationship of being a son of God would again exist in Jesus. You were either a friend, an enemy or a servant of God during these intervening years. It was radical for Jesus to refer to God as our Father to his disciples. They would have never heard anyone use such language for God.

Psalm 65:4: How blessed <835> is the one whom You (God) choose and bring near to You to dwell in Your courts. We will be satisfied with the goodness of Your house, Your holy temple. The blessed/happy person is satisfied with God’s way, even if that isn’t the way they would normally choose. Satisfaction, contentment and joy all describe scriptural happiness, and all involve that pattern of knowing AND doing what God expects from us.

Let’s expand on the basis of being sons of God – what does that entail? As sons, we find happiness in the varied sonship of others alongside of us:

1 Corinthians 12:14-18: 14 For the body is not one member, but many. 15 If the foot says, Because I am not a hand, I am not a part of the body, it is not for this reason any the less a part of the body. 16 And if the ear says, Because I am not an eye, I am not a part of the body, it is not for this reason any the less a part of the body. 17 If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the sense of smell be? 18 But now God has placed the members, each one of them, in the body, just as He desired.

How important is this group connection? Those we co-labor with in Christ go far beyond the relationship of natural families. If we do not have this co-laboring type of bond with each other and wanting to lay down our life for each other, we're missing out on this eternal relationship. When we have a good, solid relationship with someone, there is a contentment, an evenness, a trust involved. The relationship of sons of God is one that begins in this life and goes on forever. Think about the level, stable, evenness – the state of mind of working with those who think about and are drawn to what we are drawn to, those who are drawn by God through God’s spirit. It is a powerful way to find our Christian happiness. Consider this: If we are going to be spending eternity with our brotherhood, we should start getting along with them here and now. This is important!

True and sincere inclusion in any noble cause can settle anyone’s life. Inclusion into God’s own family as sons brings us a settled life with the highest of purpose and power behind it.

How well am I happily contributing to this remarkable brotherhood arrangement God gave us?

Happiness isn’t just serving God the best way we know how; it’s co-laboring with others so that collectively we can stand higher. The experience of co-laboring brings many efforts together. It is so much bigger and more effective that just our own ideas as we labor together to honor God.

Paul set the groundwork with living by the spirit and being called sons of God. Paul continues:

Romans 8:16-17: 16 The spirit himself (itself) testifies with our spirit that we are children of God, 17 and if children, heirs also, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him.

Heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ - how valuable is our inheritance? It's a gem and treasure to be with God in heaven and working with Jesus. Why? Because our inheritence is to bless all the families of the earth so they can come back into harmony with God.

This is another one of those truths we might easily skip over without realizing its monumental importance. God resurrected Jesus to a plane of existence that involves eternal life, not dependent on any outside source. That sonship we receive – being considered a child of God – provides us with the same inheritance, to be with Christ. This promise can drive us through our personal tragedies by thinking all we go through will be just a blip on the timeline of eternity.

But how often do we allow ourselves to dwell on these promises when we are engulfed in facing the difficulties of life? We can forget one of the keys to our Christian happiness – seeing things from God’s perspective.

Proverbs 29:18: Where there is no vision, the people are unrestrained, but happy<835> is he who keeps the law.

Same pattern. Same admonition. Know and do what God expects from us. Stay focused on what’s important. There may be chaos all around us, but keeping our eyes on the level path results in our happiness, our blessing.

Even when faced with torture and death, Jesus happily shared what the future would bring for his true followers:

John 14:1-3: 1 Do not let your heart be troubled; believe in God, believe also in me. 2 In my Father's house are many dwelling places; if it were not so, I would have told you; for I go to prepare a place for you. 3 If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, there you may be also.

Think about this: Jesus is about to die and says, I go to prepare a place for you. His disciples were in his heart and mind. He gave them something to look forward to, to provide that level state of mind to carry them through the coming trials. Their (and our!) happiness was important to him.

Because the unchangeableness of God’s word is a source of our happiness, we must remind ourselves who our elder brother is and how he guides, cares and protects us.

Do we happily embrace the remarkable heavenly family bond that Jesus promised?

The eighth chapter of Romans is a recipe for living a level state of mind and a happy Christian life. Having a heavenly purpose, being a son of God and having Jesus as our brother are all certainly powerful contributors to our Christian happiness! Now that we understand our spiritual family arrangement, how do we build on it as we pursue true Christian happiness?

Having such a secure family bond is a critical foundation for the kinds of experiences we will face as disciples of Jesus. In Romans 8, Paul is giving us the security of a family before he reminds us of the depth of trial and testing every follower of Jesus faces. We have something to hold on to at every level. His message should be clear: nothing can break the power of God in your life - unless you let it!

Romans 8:18: For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed to us.

How do we keep a proper attitude through suffering? By understanding that in the future we will be able to sympathize with others. We trust God that we can learn valuable life lessons for His purpose.

“You must remember that our God has all knowledge and all wisdom, and that therefore it is very possible He may guide you into paths wherein He knows great blessings are awaiting you, but which, to the shortsighted human eyes around you, seem sure to result in confusion and loss.” – The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life

Psalms 32:1-2: 1 How blessed <835> is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered! 2 How blessed <835> is the man to whom the LORD does not impute iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit! Verse 2 again (NLT): Yes, what joy for those whose record the Lord has cleared of guilt, whose lives are lived in complete honesty!

There’s a wise saying: You can’t trip over what’s behind you. Sin that has been forgiven is in the past. Often, we get stuck replaying that sin over and over because we don’t believe we have been forgiven. It’s important to learn what is necessary in order to be forgiven when we do think, say or do something we know is wrong; we know the path to forgiveness.

When we are tripping over something that's in the past, we’re sacrificing our ability to have Christian happiness in the present. We need to walk out of the past and see ourselves in the present and understand where we are going in the future. Remember Romans 8:18 above, the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed to us.

How do we get to that stage of maturity, being able to keep focused on the future? Christian happiness does not stand alone; it needs contentment.

Here is the scriptural combination that builds contentment:

1 Timothy 6:6-9: 6 But godliness actually is a means of great gain when accompanied by contentment (meaning self-satisfaction, a competence).

Great gain in these verses literally means “splendid acquisition.” Godliness can bring us “splendid acquisition” when accompanied by “spiritual competence” or contentment. 7 For we have brought nothing into the world, so we cannot take anything out of it either. 8 If we have food and covering, with these we shall be content <714>. 9 But those who want to get rich fall into temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful desires which plunge men into ruin and destruction.

Content: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #714 arkeo; a primary verb [but probably akin to #142 through the idea of raising a barrier]; properly, to ward off, i.e. (by implication) to avail (figuratively, be satisfactory) Therefore, contentment in these verses is “a spiritual competence that wards off foolish and harmful fleshly desire.” This shows how valuable contentment is in aiding our happiness.

“The teaching here is simply this, that anything allowed in the heart which is contrary to the will of God, let it seem ever so insignificant, or be ever so deeply hidden, will cause us to fall before our enemies.” – The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life

Contentment and happiness, though, are two different things. Having contentment – spiritual competence – helps in warding off temptations. It is more a state of being, whereas happiness is a state of mind. If we have the happiness state of mind, we have to put it into action. It’s not enough to just think it; we have to do it. We must actively put the two together in our Christian walk.

Contentment is a necessity for a Christian to have a happy life. In the same way that Christian happiness is not a state of euphoria or mere tolerance, contentment is not just sitting back and absorbing the trials of life. Rather, it is the strength of spiritual choice and action, to choose the acceptance of circumstances for the sake of Christ!

Does my spiritual contentment contribute to or detract from my Christian happiness? Does my spiritual contentment need an overhaul? The Apostle Paul has given us the basis of living in the spirit and having a family relationship with God to become joint heirs with Christ. He has introduced suffering and the spiritual contentment or competence to protect our spiritual happiness during suffering.

Now, a step further. Why do trials have such a powerful positiveness?

Romans 8:19-22: 19 For the anxious longing of the creation waits eagerly for the revealing of the sons of God. 20 For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of Him who subjected it, in hope 21 that the creation itself also will be set free from its slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. 22 For we know that the whole creation groans and suffers the pains of childbirth together until now.

How important is our responsibility of being sons of God before mankind becomes children of God? All of our growth and development as the sons of God now is to help be a blessing to mankind in God’s future kingdom.

Psalms 94:12-14: 12 Blessed <835> is the man whom You chasten, O LORD, and whom You teach out of Your law; 13 that You may grant him relief from the days of adversity, until a pit (figuratively meaning destruction) is dug for the wicked. 14 For the LORD will not abandon His people, nor will He forsake His inheritance.

God’s plan has a way to handle that which is ungodly. But this will happen in the future. We are assured that restitution and then reconciliation will come to all men, and that wickedness eventually ends. So, blessed/happy are we in our state of mind even before all the wickedness ends – even when things still look like they are out of control.

This is the kind of blessedness, the kind of happiness Romans 8:22 is talking about. Despite the whole creation groans and suffers the pains of childbirth together… as we see all around us, we can still find Christian happiness - not euphoria, but Christian stability – to be able to focus on what is happening in the context of God’s plan. Paul was an example of how his contentment gave him the strength to happily conquer (not just get by) all things:

Philippians 4:10-13: 10 But I rejoiced in the Lord greatly, that now at last you have revived your concern for me; indeed, you were concerned before, but you lacked opportunity. 11 Not that I speak from want, for I have learned to be content <842> in whatever circumstances I am. 12 I know how to get along with humble means, and I also know how to live in prosperity; in any and every circumstance I have learned the secret of being filled and going hungry, both of having abundance and suffering need. 13 I can do all things through him who strengthens me.

Content: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #842 autarkes; self-complacent, i.e., contented Paul describes being content, having that sense of wellbeing, of living our life in the context of God’s will. This is a beautiful teaching for us to hold onto. The strength Paul shows us is the soil in which happiness can grow, be tended and flourish. The Apostle Paul had a way of being the quiet voice in the midst of chaos. If you have ever been in a situation where people are worried and nervous and anxious, and somebody walks into the room who is calm and centered, you can see the others look at this calm presence and think, Oh wait, I can take a deep breath… In counseling, this is one of the absolute keys. No matter what somebody tells you, no matter how hard their circumstances; to have a soft, encouraging, thoughtful, non- emotional answer is a way to help them cope.

This is the Apostle Paul “walking into our room” and calming us, changing the energy, showing us exactly how to deal with too much prosperity (which believe it or not can be a real trial), or on the other end of the spectrum, too much want. The King James Version says, I know how to be abased and I know how to abound. Paul mastered what we learned from the Old Testament: be level – on even ground, go straight, advance, make progress. Look closely at Paul’s state of mind - it is content. This, in turn, gives him peace, which in turn leads to more contentment. One feeds the other. If we can master the idea of having a settled, level state of mind and apply it in a contented way towards the chaos we face, it will not only keep us balanced but can help those around us to feel calm. Think of Paul and Silas singing hymns in prison right after they were beaten in

Acts 16:16-40. They had contentment even in imprisonment! They had a positive effect on the jailer and the other prisoners.

A contented way of living our Christian life compliments the necessary, happy state of a Christian mind. The further we mature in discipleship, the more we will realize that we will not stay happy without being contented.

How often do I check in on my balance of a contented life and a happy state of mind?

I will tell you from personal experience that sometimes the answer to that question is not very good. I had an experience just this past week. I spent a lot of time preparing to visit with a client and was ready to go to meet with him. About 10 or 15 minutes before I left, he called and cancelled. I was courteous, but after I got off the phone I was griping and complaining. If he had just called earlier, I would not have wasted all that time. About 15 or 20 minutes later, I got a call from a dear sister in Christ who was having a hard time with a very difficult experience. She was looking for someone to talk to, to be that quiet voice. If I had been on that appointment, I could not have taken that call! After talking to her, I realized I just need to remember that God always has it in control. Be level, be happy, be contented because we do not know where He is bringing us.

Romans 8:23: And not only this, but also we ourselves, having the first fruits of the spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our body.

Since our experiences in the school of Christ are tough, and we can't wait for our spiritual change, what do we do? Focus on developing the fruit of the spirit, and in so doing, we will be victorious.

We asked before: does the Lord want us to be happy? Absolutely!

Isaiah 30:18: Therefore the LORD longs to be gracious to you, and therefore He waits on high to have compassion on you. For the LORD is a God of justice; how blessed <835> are all those who long for Him.

What a beautiful scripture! God longs to be gracious. He has provided an even, level road to walk on, that settled approach to life. Do we trust Him enough to stay on that road, or is there an interesting path that leads somewhere else we keep veering towards? Here’s the reward that comes after all the difficulty:

1 John 3:2-3: 2 Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not appeared as yet what we will be. We know that when he (Jesus) appears, we will be like him, because we will see him just as he is. 3 And everyone who has this hope fixed on him purifies himself, just as he is pure.

There is a beautiful anticipation of not knowing what the promised future will be like but knowing it is better than anything we could possibly ever imagine. That is what keeps our hearts and minds level in that contentment and moving forward with our Christian happiness.

Christian happiness is expanded in proportion to the focus we have on not only what God has done for us, but what He promises in the future. Such powerful anticipation can ease any trial and help reframe any confusion.

How much time do I spend thinking about my trials versus looking forward to God’s blessings?

That’s a simple but powerful question: Does my mind dwell in the anxiety of my life, or in the blessedness of what God gives me each day? For every measure of anxiety, there is a more powerful measure of grace. How am I doing balancing myself between the two? We may not be able to eliminate anxiety all at once, but we can begin to replace it with grace, piece-by-piece.

Trials, patience, perspective, understanding God’s plan for all and contentedness. These are just a few pieces of the Christian happiness puzzle!

So, what is the conclusion for all of this? How do we get Christian happiness to make a permanent home in our hearts and minds?

The possibility of a permanent happiness perspective grows along with our Christian maturity. As long as we are seeking Christlikeness, remembering our spiritual family ties and facing our trials and experiences with grace, we are on the right track.

“Remember always that there are two things which are more utterly incompatible even than oil and water, and these two are trust and worry. Can you call it trust…if day after day you are spending hours of anxious thought and questionings about the matter? When believers really trust anything, they cease to worry about the thing they have trusted.” – The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life

Next, the Apostle Paul gives us the conclusion - the absolute secret to a happy Christian life:

Romans 8:28: And we know that God causes all things to work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to His purpose.

How important is this secret of knowing that we have been called to the prize of the high calling in Christ Jesus, as described in Philippians 3:14? It means we can claim this promise as we strive to transform our lives to Christlikeness, which will bring us to victory.

Job 5:17-18: 17 Behold, how happy <835> is the man whom God reproves, so do not despise the discipline of the Almighty. 18 For He inflicts pain, and gives relief; He wounds, and His hands also heal.

In context, this is Eliphaz speaking, one of Job’s friends. He ends up getting a lot of things wrong, but the principle he brings out here is good. This is like going to a surgeon. The aftermath of surgery is often extremely painful with a slow recovery, but it is for the better good. God overrules by allowing certain trials for growth, learning, testing and making us stronger. Difficulty produces the necessary growth needed to be great. Jesus himself learned obedience from the things which he suffered (Hebrews 5:8), so why would we go through life any differently? There is power in knowing that God causes all things to work together for good to those who love Him and are called according to His purpose. Even so, for some of us, anxiety is always lurking in the background. For those who struggle with it, please do not despair. Look at this as a way to work step-by-step and build something different. Anxiety is powerful, and yet it cannot compete with the surety of God’s care.

Matthew 6:24-28 tells us we can’t serve two masters. We can’t serve God AND wealth.

We can’t add a single hour to our lives by worrying.

He continues by saying:

Matthew 6:31-33: 31 Do not worry then, saying, What will we eat? or What will we drink? or What will we wear for clothing? 32 For the Gentiles eagerly seek all these things; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. 33 But seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

I just saw a video of a pastor on stage with two tall ladders. He had one leg on each, so his legs were spread almost into the splits. One ladder he named “God’s will” and the other “My will.” He physically demonstrated that you can’t climb either one without putting both feet on one ladder. Climbing one prevents you from climbing the other. It was a great visual demonstration of trying to “serve two masters.”

Seek first His kingdom and His righteousness and everything else falls into place (Matthew 6:33).

Jesus has assured us over and over again that we, as his followers, are in the absolute focus of God’s eyes.

Believing and embracing this fact deflates the strength of our anxiety and feeds the happiness of our Christian mindset.

Am I deflating my anxieties daily, or am I regularly expanding them?

We can’t simply talk anxiety away. We can tell ourselves to stop being anxious; I know God loves me; I know there are promises…but you can’t talk anxiety away. However, talking can open the door to acting anxiety away. We can change our state of mind - happiness leads to contentment. Our state of mind leads to a state of being.

Romans 8:35-37: 35 Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? 36 Just as it is written, for your sake we are being put to death all day long; we were considered as sheep to be slaughtered. 37 But in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through him who loved us.

Since we sacrifice our wills daily to do God’s will, do we allow the trials and struggles we face to draw us closer to Jesus who loves us? If so, we truly have contentment/happiness in Christ. “Perfect obedience would be perfect happiness, if only we had perfect confidence in the power we were obeying.” - The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life Said another way, sacrifice and trials are tools of growing and showing faithfulness in Christ.

Daniel 12:12-13: 12 How blessed <835> is he who keeps waiting and attains to the 1,335 days! 13 But as for you, go your way to the end; then you will enter into rest and rise again for your allotted portion at the end of the age.

The 12th chapter of Daniel is a prophecy about the return of Christ and the events surrounding his second advent. We aren’t going to get into the math, but the point here is that Daniel was shown future events of our day that he didn’t understand. Those who would be watching for the Lord’s return would be blessed. As far as Daniel, he was assured he would die, be resurrected and receive his reward for faithfulness which we know from other scriptures is back on earth. Even under many adversities, Daniel lived a happy, contented life as a prophet of God.

This wasn’t euphoria; rather, Daniel was content from following God’s word, writing what was revealed to him and being faithful.

Back to the New Testament: Jesus did not mince words about what the life of his disciples may require. Life would be hard and they would face many challenges.

He continued with:

Matthew 10:29-31: 29 Are not two sparrows sold for a cent? And yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. 30 But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. 31 So do not fear; you are more valuable than many sparrows.

One of the concepts from The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life was that daily, without thinking, we put ourselves in the hands of others: train conductors and pilots, waiters, butchers…all who have the ability to cause us to die by crashing or poisoning us or giving us contaminated food, yet we don’t give it a second thought. But putting ourselves into the hands of the one, true, almighty God gives us pause and causes us to take back our worries to control ourselves.

This makes sense when we consider it from a spiritual perspective. The Christian’s secret to happy living is to think with that spiritual mind the apostle walked us through in Romans 8.

Having put anxiety away through the conviction of God’s care we can now be strongly positioned for a truly sacrificial life. Christian happiness actually thrives in sacrifice for we know that this is the pathway to truly conquering through our Father’s care and direction.

Do I see the power of godly sacrifice daily, or do I lean towards ways to avoid it?

There are many ways to justify doing what we want to do. But is what we are doing leading us to that happiness, to an even, level and progressing state of mind?

Romans 8:38-39: 38 For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, 39 nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Do I have such trust and conviction in God working in me to stand firm and not allow anything to separate His love and purpose for my life like Paul? If so, we have appropriate happiness. Only we can separate ourselves from the love of God.

Psalm 40:4: How blessed <835> is the man who has made the LORD his trust, and has not turned to the proud, nor to those who lapse into falsehood.

One more quote from Val, one of our CQ volunteers: “Happiness is the reality of the choice of living a joyful life. It’s 100 percent dependent on where and who your hope lies in.” Christian happiness can say it’s all good, even through difficult circumstances. Looking back, we can see how much time Jesus invested into our Christian happiness on the night before he was crucified:

John 13:12-17: 12 So when he had washed their feet, and taken his garments and reclined at the table again, he said to them, do you know what I have done to you? 13 You call me teacher and lord; and you are right, for so I am. 14 If I then, the lord and the teacher, washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.

Jesus showed us a way to be happy: wash each other’s feet. Do the kind of service that others would not think of, even if it’s lowly. Be in a position of serving others like Jesus. 15 For I gave you an example that you also should do as I did to you. 16 Truly, truly, I say to you, a slave is not greater than his master, nor is one who is sent greater than the one who sent him. 17 If you know these things, you are blessed <3107> if you do them. We are blessed and happy if we do what Jesus has told us and showed us. Through Jesus, God has called us to a life of growth, change, trial, anxiety, pain and even suffering. To be able to thrive in all of this, He gave us His son, the man Christ Jesus to show us exactly how to thrive and be happy and fulfilled in this context.

Christian happiness is not only attainable, but God expects it from us! What do I expect?

God gives us every tool conceivable to give us Christian happiness. Am I building my expectations up with what God has given or what the world imposes on me? I can choose to be happy in God through Christ or anxious in the world through Satan. Happiness is not a goal; it is a by-product. – Eleanor Roosevelt.

What will we do with what we have learned on this topic? What kind of Christian happiness decisions will I make? Happiness is not a feeling; it's a decision. It means looking at the circumstances of our lives and what we have opportunity to learn and asking how we are doing so far. It’s okay to have anxiety. Take the small steps to apply the even, level state of mind Romans 8 gives us so we can live a happy Christian life. So, is there a Christian secret to a happy life?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …think about it!

All scriptures cited are from the NASB1995 translation unless otherwise noted.
